question:
In the unit circle shown in the figure, chords \(PQ\) and \(MN\) are parallel to the unit radius \(OR\) of the circle with center at \(O.\) Chords \(MP,\) \(PQ,\) and \(NR\) are each \(s\) units long and chord \(MN\) is \(d\) units long.

[Figure 1](figures/1973_AMC_12_Q35_question_fig1.svg)

Of the three equations \[ \begin{array}{rl} \mathrm{I}.&d-s=1,\\ \mathrm{II}.&ds=1,\\ \mathrm{III}.&d^2-s^2=\sqrt5 \end{array} \] those which are necessarily true are
solution:
The parallel chords suggest using the diameter perpendicular to them. It bisects both chords, so reflection across this diameter exchanges \(M\) with \(N\) and \(P\) with \(Q\).

Let \(L\) be the point opposite \(R\) on the circle. The upper semicircle has points in the order \(L,M,P,Q,N,R\). Reflection gives \(LM=NR=s\) and \(QN=MP=s\). Together with the given equalities, the five consecutive chords on this semicircle all have length \(s\). Equal chords subtend equal minor arcs, so each of these five arcs measures \(180^\circ/5=36^\circ\). The upper arcs from \(R\) to \(P\) and from \(N\) to \(M\) each consist of three such arcs. Their chords are therefore equal, giving \(RP=MN=d\).

Now let \(H\) and \(K\) be the perpendicular projections of \(P\) and \(N\), respectively, onto the line \(OR\). Since the perpendicular diameter bisects the horizontal chords, \(H\) is on the opposite side of \(O\) from \(R\), with \(OH=s/2\), while \(OK=d/2\). The unit radii \(OP\) and \(ON\) give
\[
PH^2=1-\frac{s^2}{4},\qquad
NK^2=1-\frac{d^2}{4}.
\]
Applying the Pythagorean theorem to \(RHP\) and \(RKN\) now expresses the two chord lengths using their horizontal and vertical parts:
\[
\begin{aligned}
d^2=RP^2
&=\left(1+\frac{s}{2}\right)^2+1-\frac{s^2}{4}
=2+s,\\
s^2=RN^2
&=\left(1-\frac{d}{2}\right)^2+1-\frac{d^2}{4}
=2-d.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting these equations reveals a useful factorization:
\[
(d-s)(d+s)=d^2-s^2=d+s.
\]
Both chord lengths are positive, so \(d+s>0\), and division gives \(d-s=1\). Substituting \(d=s+1\) into \(s^2=2-d\) gives \(s^2+s=1\), hence \(ds=s(s+1)=1\). Finally,
\[
(d+s)^2=(d-s)^2+4ds=5.
\]
Since \(d+s>0\), we have \(d+s=\sqrt5\), and therefore \(d^2-s^2=(d-s)(d+s)=\sqrt5\). All three equations are true, so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
